text: Data classification means assigning every meaningful unit of data a sensitivity tier reflecting how much harm its exposure would cause — Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted, or whatever scheme fits. Those tiers only mean anything once a named data owner is accountable for deciding them, and a consistent labeling mechanism lets the tier travel with the data wherever it goes. That's why classification is an organizational exercise before it's a technical one — no tool decides your HR database is Restricted, people with authority over that data do.

Microsoft Purview Information Protection implements this as sensitivity labels, applied manually or automatically based on content inspection, embedded directly in the file so they survive downloads, email, and moves between storage systems. That persistence is what lets a Purview DLP policy act on the label directly — block external sharing of anything labeled Highly Confidential — because the label already answers how sensitive the content is before the policy has to guess.

AWS doesn't have that kind of embedded label for S3 objects, mostly because data landing there usually arrived through a pipeline, not a person saving a file. Macie approaches it from discovery instead: scanning buckets, using pattern matching and machine learning to identify sensitive content inside objects that were never manually labeled, and surfacing findings about what's there and how exposed it is. It's a continuously refreshed inventory, not a persistent label — the practical substitute when nothing was classified at creation.

Skip classification, and a DLP tool has to answer "how sensitive is this" itself, in real time, using only content inspection — regex, keyword lists, maybe a classifier. That produces exactly the failure modes you'd expect: false positives, like a training document with a sample credit card number getting blocked same as a real one, and false negatives, like a genuinely confidential strategy document with no detectable pattern sailing through untouched.

Classified first, a DLP policy's job narrows to enforcing a rule keyed to a label a human or reliable classifier already assigned — far more tractable than inferring sensitivity from content alone every single time. The practical sequence: identify data owners, define the tiers the organization actually needs, apply labels manually or through Purview and Macie, and only then write DLP policies keyed to those labels, layered on top of the access controls and encryption from earlier in this chapter.
That closes out data protection in the cloud. Chapter 7 turns to detecting and responding to cloud attacks, starting with how a leaked cloud credential actually gets abused.
